newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian leader, parties agree on new government.
newsitem.headline: Albanian leader, parties agree on new government.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha and leaders of all political parties signed an agreement on Sunday calling for a national unity government and elections by June in a bid to end an armed rebellion in the south.
The nine-point accord gave rebels holding several cities in the south a week to hand in weapons.

The agreement, clinched after two days of talks and mediation by senior European emissaries, followed Berisha's reversal of his refusal to form a coalition with the Socialists, heirs to Albania's Communist party that ruled for five decades.
The June deadline for fresh elections was a further concession to the opposition. Berisha had initially proposed new polls within 45 days and then extended this to two months.
The opposition, which criticised last May's election as unfair, had objected to such a short time frame, saying it was impossible to hold polls under a state of emergency introduced last week.
More than 20 people have died in the latest wave of violence in Albania, initially sparked by the collapse of fraudulent investment schemes that left small savers penniless.

In a meeting with political parties earlier, opposition leaders praised Berisha's proposals and sought assurances that he had dropped his objections to dealing with the Socialists. Berisha had said the statutes of his Democratic Party barred coalitions with former communists.
"I meant all parties seated here. It's clear," Berisha said during the meeting, conveyed to Albania's 3.4 million people in a highly unusual television broadcast.
"Last night I was categorical about the Socialist Party. But there are moral considerations...a moral obligation. Sometimes, you have to choose morals over laws."
However rebel leaders in the southern town of Gjirokaster indicated they would not consider any arms amnesty unless it involved the resignation of Berisha.

Rebels accuse the Albanian leader of standing by while thousands of Albanians lost their life savings in a series of schemes that collapsed in January, sparking the initial unrest that turned into an anti-government uprising in the south.

The head of a European mediation mission on Saturday urged Berisha to prolong a 48-hour amnesty which ran out early on Sunday to give more time for talks and for the surrender of thousands of weapons seized by the rebels from army depots.
In Gjirokaster, which fell to the rebels on Saturday, retired army general Agim Gozhita took charge on Sunday, ordering teenagers to hand in their weapons and vowing to punish looters.

One person was killed and three were wounded during a night of wild celebrations after rebels seized the town, site of the main army base for the region. Army reinforcements flown in to defend it fled to the mountains.

"There will be no more shootings. Children under 18 should not carry weapons. Shops will open and those caught stealing will be punished," Gozhita told a crowd of 1,500 after he was elected president of the town's 15-member rebel council.
In other southern towns still under government control no major incidents were reported by residents reached by telephone, but the mood was described as tense and most people were staying indoors.
In the town of Ballsh, some 120 kms (75 miles) south of Tirana, journalists reported four government tanks drawn up around the country's main oil refinery built by the Chinese.
Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini was reported to be flying to Tirana on Sunday night to discuss with Berisha "how to move ahead to democratic elections", an Italian government spokesman said.
